Central idea of *The Deserted Village* (Oliver Goldsmith, 1770)
The poem is a lament for the decline of rural village life in England. Goldsmith blames the social and economic changes of his time, especially:
Enclosure of common land. Wealthy landlords took over land that villagers had farmed, and the peasants were evicted.
Rural depopulation. Villagers were forced to emigrate or move to cities, so the village ("Sweet Auburn") became empty.
Greed and luxury versus simple virtue. Goldsmith contrasts the wealth of the rich with the contentment, honesty and community of the poor.
Loss of a happy, innocent way of life. He remembers the village's pastimes, the kind preacher, the schoolmaster and the alehouse, all of which are now gone.
Warning to the nation. He argues that a country loses its strength and moral character when its peasantry is destroyed to make a few people richer.
Common themes
Nostalgia for a lost past
Criticism of materialism and inequality
Sympathy for the poor
The value of rural simplicity and community
Frequently quoted lines and what they mean
*"Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, / Where wealth accumulates, and men decay."* A nation suffers when wealth grows while its people are degraded.
*"Sweet Auburn! loveliest village of the plain..."* This opens the poem with a fond memory of the village's former happiness.
*"A time there was, ere England's griefs began..."* This recalls a past when people lived in contentment.
